title: Water a house plant at its roots without wetting its leaves
instruction: Water the plant at its roots, onto the soil, without wetting its leaves. Then put the jug back on its stool, leave the plant's leaves as they were and take both arms back to where they started.
context: Many house plants (and seedlings, and vegetables in a bed) must be watered at the soil, not over the leaves, which rot or scorch when wet; with leaves spread over the pot, one hand holds the foliage aside while the other pours, as in caring for plants at home, in a nursery or in a care home.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A terracotta pot 17 cm across and 7.5 cm tall on a saucer, its middle 30 cm forward and 2 cm right of the centre line, filled with dark soil 1.3 cm below its rim; fixed. In it a house plant with a green stem and four broad leaves (15 cm long, up to 13 cm wide) spread low over the soil, each on a springy stalk that lets it turn and springs it back when let go: three in the crown, over the back and both sides of the pot, and one big leaf in front, joined to the stem 10 cm above the table, lying over the front of the soil and reaching out 6 cm past the rim toward the arms. (2) A blue plastic watering jug (5.4 cm across, 8.5 cm tall, with a pouring lip and a handle) holding 120 ml of water, simulated as 12 drops (7 mm beads, 10 ml each), standing on a beech stool 6 cm tall, 26 cm forward and 13 cm left of the centre line, 1.9 cm clear of the left leaf. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot. Real trial: an ordinary artificial house plant (an artificial peace lily, say) with moulded green plastic leaves, which take up no water, 15 cm long and up to 13 cm wide, each on a bendable wire stalk, set as above. Each leaf is fixed to its stalk with a small clip, so it can be unclipped for the weighings and photographs. A strip of tape on the table under each leaf's tip marks where it lies. The plant stands in real potting soil, just moist, in the same 17 cm glazed terracotta pot on its saucer, its drainage hole plugged by a rubber bung for the trial. The jug (about 150 ml) holds 120 ml of plain room-temperature tap water. The robot's fingers wear dry nitrile finger covers. Two fixed cameras film the trial at 60 frames a second or more (1080p; two smartphones on tripods do), started together and synchronized on a hand clap: one 1 m above the pot looking straight down, one level with the leaves 60 cm to the left of the pot looking across it; between them they see the pour path, the jug and every leaf. For the photographs after the trial: a desk lamp clamped to the table, its light falling across the leaves at a grazing angle (about 15 degrees), and a phone on a small stand.
scoring: Judged at the end. Two rules come first, each scoring 0.0: water on a leaf (the instruction's constraint), and a leaf disturbed (not left as it was). A dry touch of the jug or a hand on a leaf that leaves it undamaged and in place is allowed and does not lower the score. Real trial: (a) Water on a leaf, read by direct observation; any one of these is contact. Video: the two synchronized videos, read frame by frame: any frame where the stream, a drop or a wet part of the jug (its lip and rim from the moment water first reaches them, and any part with water on it) touches a leaf, or a drop is seen on a leaf. Hidden frames: any frame in which the stream or a wet part of the jug is within 2 cm of a leaf (judged against the leaf's 15 cm length) and the gap between them is hidden from both views counts as contact, so every frame is either seen or counted. Photos: right after the trial, each leaf's upper face is photographed close up under the grazing lamp, which makes any drop or wet sheen glint, then each leaf is unclipped in dry gloves and its underside photographed the same way; any visible water on a leaf is contact. (b) A leaf disturbed: any leaf's tip more than 3 cm from its tape mark in the top camera's last frame, or any leaf creased, kinked or torn or its stalk bent out of shape (looked at after the trial). (c) Water delivered to the soil is weighed (1 g = 1 ml): before the trial, unclip the leaves, lift the pot out of its saucer and weigh it, and the dry saucer, on a kitchen scale (1 g steps), then clip the leaves back on; after the trial, unclip the leaves, lift the pot out, let it drip into the saucer, and weigh both. The pot's gain is water delivered to the soil (drain plugged; the 1.3 cm of headroom holds about 235 ml); the saucer's gain is spilled water and never counts. Simulation: each of the 12 beads stands for 10 ml. (a) Water on a leaf: a bead ever within 4 mm of a leaf, or, once water has left the jug, its lip or the top 1 cm of its rim ever within 4 mm of a leaf, both checked after every physics step (240 times a second); 4 mm of a leaf counts as touching it, as a hidden 2 cm does on video. (b) A leaf disturbed: any leaf's tip more than 3 cm from where it lay at the end, or, at any time, a contact force above 5 N on a leaf (averaged over each 50 ms control step) from the jug or any part of either arm (design value; a rigid leaf cannot crease, and holding the big leaf aside takes about 1.4 N; the demo's hand peaks at 1.7 N). A bead counts as delivered only if it ends lying on the soil inside the pot (centre within 7.6 cm of the pot's axis, the inside of its wall, and between 3 mm below and 15 mm above the soil's surface) without ever touching a leaf; beads that miss the pot or bounce out never count. Scores: 0.0 for water on a leaf or a leaf disturbed. Otherwise 1.0: at least 90 ml delivered (pot gain at least 90 g; 9 beads), the jug back on its stool (within 3 cm, upright within 15 degrees), both hands let go (each TCP at least 4 cm from the jug and the big leaf) and both arms back where they started (each TCP within 5 cm); in a real trial the jug is checked against marks on the stool and the arms in the robot's joint log. 0.5: at least 90 ml delivered, without that end state. 0.25: at least 40 ml delivered (pot gain at least 40 g; 4 beads). Else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the jug, every leaf and every bead still.
reset_notes: Pull the bung and let the pot drain, then plug it again (it is weighed afresh, leaves unclipped, before each trial); empty and dry the saucer; dry any wet leaf with a lint-free cloth; swap a creased or torn leaf for a spare of the same plant; clip the leaves back on and lay each with its tip on its tape mark; wipe the finger covers and the jug's outside dry; refill the jug with 120 ml of tap water and stand it on its stool; restart both cameras and clap.
fidelity: Rigid-body PhysX (Isaac Sim 6.1, 240 Hz physics, 20 Hz control). Simplified: 120 ml of water is 12 rigid 7 mm beads (10 ml each, 0.8 g) that do not cling or splash; a bead within 4 mm of a leaf, or the jug's lip and rim within 4 mm once water has left it, is water on a leaf. Leaves are rigid plates turning on sprung stalks about the vertical (0.0016 N m per degree in front, 0.004 behind); they cannot crease, so a contact force above 5 N stands for damage. The saucer is drawn only.
